item.title: Enforcing Axioms for AI Alignment under Loss-Based Rules
item.description: arXiv:2611.13369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many alignment methods, most notably reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), train reward models by minimizing a loss on pairwise comparisons of model responses. Inspired by principle-guided methods such as Constitutional AI, we treat each principle as a voter that compares responses according to that principle, for example, preferring the more helpful or less toxic response. We represent these voters as linear directions in a fixed embedding space, a simplifying assumption motivated by the Linear Representation Hypothesis. In this linear social choice model, Ge et al. (2024) showed that an optimal linear reward model can violate Pareto optimality (PO): From the principles-as-voters lens, this means a response A can be less helpful and more toxic than B, yet still receive a higher reward. We ask whether richer reward models or changes to comparison data can recover PO within loss-based training. We show that PO can still fail for polynomials of any fixed degree and one-hidden-layer ReLU multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) of any fixed width $ d\ge 2 $ with suitable finite parameter bounds. We then recover PO for loss-based training of linear rewards under suitable assumptions in an idealized setting with uniform comparison directions and equal comparison lengths. These results motivate dataset design as an approach to recovering PO in constitutional-style alignment while retaining loss-based training.
item.dc:creator: Alexandros Hollender, Sonja Kraiczy

item.title: Adversarial risk analysis with fully probabilistic designs
item.description: arXiv:2611.14289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adversarial risk analysis (ARA) informs decision-makers when facing intelligent opponents and uncertain outcomes, enabling an analyst to model beliefs about the opponents' preferences, capabilities, beliefs, and the strategic calculations that opponents employ. Major applications cover reliability and risk analysis of critical infrastructures in presence of adversarial threats. In such domains, ARA mitigates typical common knowledge assumptions of standard game-theoretic approaches. However, ARA entails complex modelling and computations. To alleviate these, we explore its combination with fully probabilistic design (FPD), a control theory methodology supporting an agent in choosing the decision distribution that achieves the outcomes with a distribution closest to its ideal. We use FPD to model and forecast the opponent's decisions within an ARA setting and present how to handle security games within this ARA-FPD framework, covering both single and multiple stage problems.
item.dc:creator: Mario Chac\'on-Falc\'on, Tatiana Valentine Guy, Miroslav K\'arn\'y, David Rios Insua

item.title: Second-Best Trade Is Half Efficient in Multidimensional Markets
item.description: arXiv:2611.14489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that at least half of the first-best gains from trade can always be achieved in multidimensional two-sided markets with additive values and costs and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints. The guarantee is achieved by a mechanism satisfying Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality, and strong budget balance, and is tight already in single-item bilateral trade. Types are independent across agents, while the coordinates of each agent's type may be arbitrarily correlated. Feasibility constraints may couple trades across items and agents. This extends the known tight one-half guarantee for single-item bilateral trade. Our proof develops a new application of the Cai--Devanur--Weinberg duality framework. We show that the objective of every feasible dual is at least half of the first best. Strong duality then yields the guarantee without characterizing an optimal mechanism or dual. The key observation is that every feasible dual induces continuous-time Markov chains that, when stopped by exponential clocks, recover true types as expectations of virtual types. The dual constraints control the rate at which these chains change the prior distributions. We establish our bound by combining this control with a coupling of the agents' clocks.
item.dc:creator: Dirk Bergemann, Yang Cai, Kangning Wang, Jinzhao Wu, Renzhe Xu

item.title: Artificial Currency and Separate Selling: A 3-Approximation for Consumer Surplus
item.description: arXiv:2611.14509v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the allocation of indivisible items to buyers with additive values drawn from independent distributions. The objective is consumer surplus net of burnt payments. We consider artificial-currency mechanisms: buyers receive personalized budgets of a currency worthless outside the mechanism and use them to bid across items. The better of separate selling and artificial-currency mechanisms provides a 3-approximation to optimal consumer surplus. The guarantee holds at every Bayes--Nash equilibrium, without equilibrium selection. Both branches are necessary: either alone may capture only a vanishing share of the optimum. The proof decomposes benchmark surplus into a stable part captured by artificial currency and a variation covered by separate selling.
item.dc:creator: Yang Cai, Yingkai Li, Jinzhao Wu

item.title: Elicitation of the parameters of a multi-criteria sorting model
item.description: arXiv:2611.13062v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multiple-criteria decision aiding (MCDA) proposes models and methods for different types of decision problems such as choice, ranking or sorting. Such models involve various parameters that must be elicited. In the elicitation process, all necessary information has to be taken from the decision-maker. For this, several direct and indirect elicitation methods are suggested in the literature. In this work, we concentrate on direct elicitation: we aim at providing a rigorous elicitation procedure for the parameters of the Non-Compensatory Sorting model (NCS), which has been characterized by an axiomatic analysis. A basic version of the NCS model is considered, i.e., a model with two categories and no vetoes. The parameters are the set of sufficient coalitions of criteria and the profile separating the two categories. Regarding the sufficient coalitions, we propose several questioning algorithms that engraft questions on classical graph exploration algorithms such as depth-first search. Such algorithms are implemented and evaluated by simulation. For eliciting the limit profile, we design a questioning algorithm using dichotomy. Questioning algorithms can be optimal in the worst case or on average. An optimal algorithm in the worst case has been proposed by Hansel in the framework of monotone Boolean functions. We implement and evaluate this algorithm as a variant of the depth-first search approaches. Regarding optimal questioning strategies on average, we evaluate decision trees for up to four criteria. On the other hand, we assess how more general is NCS as compared to MR-Sort, a particular case of the NCS model in which sufficient coalitions can be represented by additive weights.
item.dc:creator: Eda Ersek Uyanik

item.title: Useful Work Can Increase Energy Use: Demand Elasticity and Proof of Useful Work
item.description: arXiv:2611.13131v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A serious criticism of Bitcoin's Proof-of-Work is its enormous electricity consumption. Proof-of-Useful-Work (PoUW), introduced by Ball, Rosen, Sabin, and Vasudevan (2017), in which mining performs useful computations, was suggested as an alternative to reduce electricity expenditure, with matrix multiplication (MatMul) as a recent concrete instantiation by Komargodski and Weinstein (2026). Perhaps surprisingly, we show that switching to PoUW may increase the total electricity consumption, echoing Jevons' paradox. Intuitively, the PoUW mechanism acts as a subsidy that lowers the effective price of the useful work. Recall that demand is elastic if a discount of x percent in the price leads to an increase of more than x percent in the quantity demanded. If demand is elastic, the resulting increase in quantity demanded leads to a net increase in total electricity consumption; if inelastic, total electricity consumption decreases. Even then, the electricity consumption due to PoUW never vanishes, since the mining subsidy is spent on useful work that would not have been produced without the subsidy. This result is proved in a simple model with electricity-only costs, no PoUW overhead, and an unchanged mining subsidy. The analysis extends to less restrictive settings with adjusted thresholds.
item.dc:creator: Isaiah Hull, Or Sattath

item.title: An Improved $(1+2e)$-Approximation Algorithm for Metric Data Placement
item.description: arXiv:2611.13224v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the metric data placement problem with site-capacity constraints and fixed installation costs, aiming to minimize the total cost of placing data (resources) and accessing their nearest copies. We develop a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm based on a natural linear programming relaxation of the problem. Starting from an optimal fractional solution, we construct multiscale metric-ball partitions independently for each resource and connect overlapping balls at consecutive levels to form a flow network. The resource layers are then coupled through shared site-capacity arcs, allowing us to obtain an integral placement by minimizing a surrogate cost over a single min-cost circulation. By optimizing the choice of ball radii, we establish an approximation factor of $1+2e\approx 6.44$. To our knowledge, this is the best approximation guarantee for the metric data placement problem since its introduction by Baev and Rajaraman in 2001.
item.dc:creator: S. Rasoul Etesami

item.title: Dynamic investment and coordination in teams: Theory and experimental evidence
item.description: arXiv:2611.13230v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Teamwork requires more than the general skills that team members bring. In successful teams, members invest in team-specific skill or capital that accumulates within the team and raises the return to coordinated production. We provide the first systematic analysis of dynamic investment in such team skill. Adopting a dynamic game approach, we develop a novel theoretical framework where investment in team skill creates persistent benefits but is risky because the benefits depend on successful team coordination. We then take this framework to the laboratory to study empirically the factors that influence dynamic investment in team skill. We find underinvestment compared to the efficient benchmark. However, investment responds strongly to incentives, in line with specific theory-predicted patterns. Pre-registered traits (theory of mind and propensity to coordinate) predict investment and team-level efficiency. We conclude that careful design of team incentives and selection of team members can facilitate the development of team skill.
item.dc:creator: David Gill, Victoria Prowse, J. Lucas Reddinger

item.title: Splitting for Stability: a Modified Reward Scheme for Transaction-Fee-Only Regimes
item.description: arXiv:2611.13252v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As Bitcoin's block subsidy declines over time, miner revenue will come to depend increasingly on transaction fees. In fee-dominated regimes, winner-take-all reward structures can create incentives for undercutting and fork-based mining strategies, leading to instability and reduced transaction throughput. To prevent this instability, we propose a reward-splitting mechanism in which the winning block producer receives an $\alpha$-portion of the block reward, while the rest is distributed among other miners; this incentivizes mining on previous blocks with higher rewards, while preserving the incentive to produce blocks with high rewards. We evaluate the proposed reward structure through analysis and simulation. Our analysis derives a local profitability condition for one-step Function-Fork deviations, showing how the winner-side reward, loser-side subsidy, and honest hash power jointly determine whether undercutting is profitable. Simulations show parameter regions in which honest behavior dominates fork-based deviations. In the cases where forking becomes dominant, the learned strategy is the least aggressive variant studied. The analysis and simulations suggest that suitable reward-splitting parameters can reduce the honest participation needed to suppress aggressive forking strategies relative to the winner-take-all structure studied in prior work. Finally, we show that the modified reward scheme does not appear to worsen selfish mining incentives. Together, these results suggest that reward redistribution can mitigate fee-driven fork incentives without introducing stronger selfish mining incentives, providing a possible direction for incentive design in fee-era proof-of-work systems.
item.dc:creator: Eric Brigham, Baigang Chen, Nicholas Hopper

item.title: Choosing Complexity: Cognitive Ability, Overconfidence, and Task Choice
item.description: arXiv:2611.13259v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Workers and organizations routinely choose between complex tasks that differ in their success-payment tradeoff. We study how cognitive ability and overconfidence shape this choice of task complexity, both theoretically and experimentally. Consistent with our model, we find that more cognitively able individuals choose more complex tasks. Conditional on cognitive ability, we find that more overconfident individuals also choose more complex tasks. In about 75% of the decisions, subjects pick their payoff-maximizing task, and higher cognitive ability is weakly associated with more efficient choices of task complexity. But errors are strikingly one-sided: those who fail to choose optimally pick tasks that are too complex. Our findings suggest that organizations should pair task menus and incentives for choosing more complex tasks with information and feedback that help workers assess their ability and probability of success. This preserves the benefits of self-selection while reducing costly overreach.
item.dc:creator: David Gill, Zhongheng Qiao

item.title: Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization for Bounded-Payoff Imperfect-Information Games
item.description: arXiv:2611.14182v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization over the years has proven effective for approximating Nash equilibria, but Monte Carlo variants create a large overhead of sampling costs when the counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories. We propose a novel Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, a framework that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to reduce the computational complexity of the regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games, while preserving the convergence of its classical counterpart. We give a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound, discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants, the structure of their resource requirements, and outline what is needed to validate the potential advantage empirically.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Maresch, Erik Schulze, Jnan Yalla

item.title: Nash Incentive-compatible Online Mechanism Learning via Weakly Differentially Private Online Learning
item.description: arXiv:2407.04898v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a multi-round mechanism design problem, where we interact with a set of agents over a sequence of rounds. We wish to design an incentive-compatible (IC) online learning scheme to maximize an application-specific objective within a given class of mechanisms, without prior knowledge of the agents' type distributions. Even if each mechanism in this class is IC in a single round, if an algorithm naively chooses from this class on each round, the entire learning process may not be IC against non-myopic buyers who appear over multiple rounds. On each round, our method randomly chooses between the recommendation of a weakly differentially private online learning algorithm (e.g., Hedge), and a commitment mechanism which penalizes non-truthful behavior. Our method is IC and achieves $O(T^{\frac{1+h}{2}})$ regret for the application-specific objective in an adversarial setting, where $h$ quantifies the long-sightedness of the agents. When compared to prior work, our approach is conceptually simpler,it applies to general mechanism design problems (beyond auctions), and its regret scales gracefully with the size of the mechanism class.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235:20643-20659, 2024
item.dc:creator: Joon Suk Huh, Kirthevasan Kandasamy

item.title: On the Theoretical Foundations of Data Exchange Economies
item.description: arXiv:2412.01968v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Organizations increasingly seek to share and access datasets to improve their ML models and derive insights. Despite the immense demand for quality data, data exchange and collaboration have not reached their full potential, as cited by the European Commission. One of the key reasons is the lack of reciprocity, where some participants perceive their contribution to others to be of higher value than what they receive in return. We propose a general framework for data exchange without payments, focusing on two main properties: (i) reciprocal fairness, which ensures that each agent receives utility proportional to their contribution to the total welfare -- contributions are quantifiable using well-established credit-sharing functions such as the Shapley share and proportional share, and (ii) core-stability, which guarantees that no coalition of agents can identify an exchange among themselves which they all unanimously prefer to the current exchange. Surprisingly, we show that fair and stable exchanges exist for all monotone continuous utility functions. Building on this, we investigate the computational complexity of finding approximate fair and stable exchanges. We present a local search algorithm for instances with monotone submodular utility functions and cross-monotone credit-sharing functions, e.g., Shapley share. We prove that this problem belongs to CLS ($=$ PPAD $\cap$ PLS) under mild assumptions. Our framework opens up several intriguing theoretical avenues for future research on data economics.
item.dc:creator: Hannaneh Akrami, Bhaskar Ray Chaudhury, Jugal Garg, Aniket Murhekar

item.title: Pandora's Knapsack via Simple Policies
item.description: arXiv:2509.05956v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Pandora's Knapsack: a hybrid of the classic stochastic knapsack [Dean, Goemans, and Vondr'ak, 2008] and Pandora's box [Weitzman, 1979]. As in stochastic knapsack, items have sizes drawn from known distributions, and items that fit within a knapsack contribute to the total value. As in Pandora, every item $i$ comes in a box that costs $c_i$ to open. What distinguishes our problem is that the size is revealed only after opening the box and paying the cost. A motivating application from contract design is knapsack contracts, where a principal sequentially delegates jobs with stochastic processing times to agents before a deadline, and must pay each agent to incentivize effort, even if the job ends up not completing in time. We study the power of simple decision-making policies to approximate Pandora's Knapsack, along two complexity axes: (i)~knowledge of size distributions, and (ii)~adaptivity. We show that, compared to the classic stochastic knapsack and Pandora's box, policies in our model must be significantly more complex along both axes to be approximately optimal. Conversely, we show that with full distributional information and by allowing adaptive skipping of items, a constant approximation can be recovered. Our analysis reveals an economic quantity, namely ROI (return-on-investment, defined as the jobs' minimum utility over cost), which smoothly characterizes the performance of simple policies. Across a hierarchy of increasingly adaptive policies, we establish tight adaptivity gaps all governed by ROI. To demonstrate the importance of the ROI parameter in characterizing simple policies, we revisit Pandora's box, and show that return-on-investment exactly captures the adaptivity gap in this classic problem as well.
item.dc:creator: Zohar Barak, Asnat Berlin, Ilan Reuven Cohen, Alon Eden, Omri Porat, Inbal Talgam-Cohen

item.title: Is Online Linear Optimization Sufficient for Strategic Robustness?
item.description: arXiv:2602.12253v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider bidding in repeated Bayesian first-price auctions. Bidding algorithms that achieve optimal regret have been extensively studied, but their strategic robustness to the seller's manipulation remains relatively underexplored. Bidding algorithms based on no-swap-regret algorithms achieve both desirable properties, but are suboptimal in terms of statistical and computational efficiency. In contrast, online gradient ascent is the only algorithm that achieves $O(\sqrt{TK})$ regret and strategic robustness [KSS24], where $T$ denotes the number of auctions and $K$ the number of bids. In this paper, we explore whether simple online linear optimization (OLO) algorithms suffice for bidding algorithms with both desirable properties. Our main result shows that sublinear linearized regret is sufficient for strategic robustness. Specifically, we construct simple black-box reductions that convert any OLO algorithm into a strategically robust no-regret bidding algorithm, in both known and unknown value distribution settings. For the known value distribution case, our reduction yields a bidding algorithm that achieves $O(\sqrt{T \log K})$ regret and strategic robustness (with exponential improvement on the $K$-dependence compared to [KSS24]). Moreover, we can further exploit the single-strategy benchmark and construct a bidding algorithm with $O(\sqrt{T(\log K+\log T)})$ regret and $O(1)$ strategic robustness. For the unknown value distribution case, our reduction gives a bidding algorithm with high-probability $O(\sqrt{T (\log K+\log(T/\delta)})$ regret and strategic robustness, while removing the bounded density assumption made in [KSS24].
item.dc:creator: Yang Cai, Haipeng Luo, Chen-Yu Wei, Weiqiang Zheng

item.title: How Many Votes is a Lie Worth? Measuring Strategyproofness through Resource Augmentation
item.description: arXiv:2602.22838v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It is well known, by the Gibbard-Satterthwaite Theorem, that when there are more than two candidates, any non-dictatorial voting rule can be manipulated by untruthful voters. But how much stronger is an untruthful voter than a truthful one under different voting rules? We suggest measuring the potential comparative advantage of a strategic voter by asking how many copies of their (truthful) vote must be added to the election in order to achieve an outcome as good as their best manipulation. Intuitively, this definition quantifies what a voter can gain by manipulating in comparison to what they would have gained by finding like-minded voters to join the election (equivalently, by increasing their voter weight). Our measure is prior-free and requires no assumptions on the voters' cardinal utilities. Using this framework, we obtain a principled method to compare the manipulation leverage for different voting rules. We show that while the manipulation leverage of many rules grows linearly with the number of voters, Borda Count's is m-2, where m is the number of candidates. We prove that the positional scoring rule with the smallest manipulation leverage is always Borda Count (if voters outnumber candidates) or Plurality (otherwise). Further, any rule satisfying a weak form of majority consistency (and thus any Condorcet extension) cannot outperform Plurality, while any majoritarian rule will perform significantly worse. Consequently, Borda Count has much lower manipulation leverage than these wide classes of rules under large electorates. Finally, we establish a quantitative extension of the Gibbard--Satterthwaite theorem, proving no anonymous and onto voting rule can have manipulation leverage that is lower than m-2 across all electorate sizes. As a result, Borda Count is indeed optimal among all such rules.
item.dc:creator: Ratip Emin Berker, Vincent Conitzer, Eden Hartman, Jiayuan Liu, Caspar Oesterheld

item.title: EFX Need Not Exist
item.description: arXiv:2604.18216v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The existence of envy-free up to any good (EFX) allocations has long been a central open problem in discrete fair division. We resolve it in the negative by constructing a counterexample with three agents and eight goods. The instance is invariant under every simultaneous permutation of the agents and their associated good types, and this symmetry yields a short, self-contained proof of nonexistence. The counterexample can be realized with weighted-coverage, and hence submodular, valuations, and it extends to $n$ agents and $m$ goods for all $n\ge3$ and $m\ge n+5$. For three agents, eight goods is the minimum: every instance with three agents and at most seven goods admits an EFX allocation under arbitrary monotone valuations. The proof relies on a new analysis, valid for any number of goods, of when the invariant-based technique of [AACGMM25] produces an EFX allocation. This analysis strictly extends the class of MMS-feasible valuations. We also give explicit bounds for approximate EFX. For subadditive valuations, $\alpha$-EFX allocations need not exist for any $\alpha>2^{-1/6}\approx0.891$, and for submodular valuations for any $\alpha>0.958$. On the positive side, if two of three agents have arbitrary monotone valuations and the third has a subadditive valuation, there is always an allocation that is EFX for the first two and $2^{-1/3}$-EFX ($\approx0.794$) for the third. A first version of the counterexample and of the seven-goods result was obtained using SAT/SMT solving, and the insights it provided guided our classical, pen-and-paper proofs. We also describe the encoding, which we believe is a valuable tool in its own right: to our knowledge, this is the first use of SAT/SMT solving for EFX.
item.dc:creator: Hannaneh Akrami, Simon Mackenzie, Alexander Mayorov, Kurt Mehlhorn, Shreyas Srinivas, Mashbat Suzuki, Christoph Weidenbach

item.title: Sequential Phragm\'en Guarantees 2-Approximate Core Stability
item.description: arXiv:2609.29646v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study approximately stable committee selection under approval preferences, following Cheng et al.~[EC~2019] and Jiang, Munagala, and Wang~[STOC~2020]. In an approval-based committee election, $n$ voters each approve a subset of the candidates, and a committee of size $k$ is selected. A size-$k$ committee is $\lambda$-stable if, for every nonempty subset $T$ of candidates, the number of voters who strictly prefer $T$ is less than $\lambda$ times the proportional share $\frac{n|T|}{k}$. We consider sequential Phragm\'en, a classical polynomial-time voting rule, and prove that it always returns a $2$-stable committee. This implies that the $2$-core is always nonempty and improves upon the $3.651$-stability guarantee of Gao, Sun, and Vondr\'ak~[EC~2026]. The guarantee also extends to weighted voters and is tight even for unweighted elections: for every $1\le\lambda<2$, sequential Phragm\'en can return a committee that is not $\lambda$-stable. Compared with the exact-core algorithm developed in concurrent work by Becker, Greger, and Peters~[arXiv~2026], sequential Phragm\'en is simpler to implement, and our proof of its $2$-stability is elementary.
item.dc:creator: Jianan Lin, Chenhao Wang

item.title: The Query Complexity of Envy-Free Division: Cake, Chores, and Mixed Resources
item.description: arXiv:2611.11424v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the query complexity of envy-free division for cake, chores, and resources with both positive and negative values. For arbitrary nonnegative nonatomic chore costs, we give a deterministic exact protocol using $2^{n\log_2 n+O(n)}$ queries and cuts. For both cake and chores, a Las Vegas protocol uses $O(n^{12}\log(2n))$ expected queries and $O(n^{11}\log(2n))$ expected cuts. Conversely, every exact protocol with fixed positive success probability requires $\Omega(n^2)$ expected queries in general, even with arbitrarily many output cuts at no query cost. For mixed cake and chores, no uniform finite expected-query bound exists even when every Cut returns the leftmost root or every Cut returns the rightmost root. This holds for any fixed positive multiplicative approximation factor and success probability, already when all net totals are one. An additive impossibility holds on the same normalized domain.
item.dc:creator: Alireza Farhadi, Mohammadtaghi Hajiaghayi

item.title: Bandit Profit-maximization for Targeted Marketing
item.description: arXiv:2403.01361v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study a sequential profit-maximization problem, optimizing for both price and ancillary variables like marketing expenditures. Specifically, we aim to maximize profit over an arbitrary sequence of multiple demand curves, each dependent on a distinct ancillary variable, but sharing the same price. A prototypical example is targeted marketing, where a firm (seller) wishes to sell a product over multiple markets. The firm may invest different marketing expenditures for different markets to optimize customer acquisition, but must maintain the same price across all markets. Moreover, markets may have heterogeneous demand curves, each responding to prices and marketing expenditures differently. The firm's objective is to maximize its gross profit, the total revenue minus marketing costs. Our results are near-optimal algorithms for this class of problems in an adversarial bandit setting, where demand curves are arbitrary non-adaptive sequences, and the firm observes only noisy evaluations of chosen points on the demand curves. For $n$ demand curves (markets), we prove a regret upper bound of $\tilde{O}(nT^{3/4})$ and a lower bound of $\Omega((nT)^{3/4})$ for monotonic demand curves, and a regret bound of $\tilde{\Theta}(nT^{2/3})$ for demand curves that are monotonic in price and concave in the ancillary variables.
item.dc:creator: Joon Suk Huh, Ellen Vitercik, Kirthevasan Kandasamy
